newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices rise further, soybeans also gain.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices rise further, soybeans also gain.

text.p: Coffee prices rose in nervous trading on Monday after news that a fire at a warehouse in Costa Rica had destroyed stockpiled coffee.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee for May delivery closed up 3.35 cents a pound at 250.90 cents.

Costa Rica is a producer of the mild arabica coffee most in demand from U.S. coffee roasters. Though the amount of coffee lost in the warehouse fire was probably not great, the incident once more caused worries about tight coffee stocks.

"Although we have not been able to quantify the damage, neither the buildings nor the amount of coffee destroyed, we can say that the coffee losses are much less than the 50,000 bags being talked about," said Luis Diego Sanchez, manager at the Federacion de Cooperativos de Caficultores in San Jose.
Last week the May coffee contract rose to a high of 255.00 cents, the highest price for coffee since a freeze damaged Brazil's crop in July, 1994.

Coffee prices have risen 150 percent since early December as worries mounted about small crops in South America this year and possible lower production in Brazil, the top grower. Coffee roasters have been buying hand-to-mouth for weeks.
Meanwhile, stockpiles of coffee continue to shrink.

The exchange reported on Friday that coffee in warehouses certified for delivery against futures fell by 750 bags to 42,918 bags as of May 1. That amount was about half the level of a month ago; each bag weighs 132 pounds.

That amount of coffee -- the equivalent of about 152 futures contracts -- also compared to the 1,276 contracts still open for potential delivery in the May position as of Friday. The May contract expires in two weeks.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybean prices topped the $9 mark for the first time since the 1988 drought in the Midwest. But a slowdown in exports kept price gains modest.
Soybeans for May delivery closed up 5-1/2 cents a bushel at $8.93 after rising to a day's high of $9.02.
Traders remain bullish on soybean prices given continuing strong demand from domestic processors and exporters. A cold spring and planting delays have also encouraged supply worry.
But the Agriculture Department on Monday said a total of only 5.988 million bushels of soybeans were inspected for loading onto vessels for export in the week to May 1.
Traders had expected 10 million to 14 million bushels.
"The need to ration demand was the central issue going into the rally," said Mark Weidner, oilseeds analyst with Cargill Investor Services.
"When we had inspections numbers that questioned if we've actually rationed demand, that took some of the wind out of the sails. But one inspection number doesn't confirm the sales are slowing down."

Corn prices closed lower amid rapid planting progress over the weekend in the Midwest. The Agriculture Department said that 50 percent of the corn crop was planted as of Sunday, compared to 18 percent a week ago and 40 percent a year ago.
Corn for May delivery ended 1-3/4 cents a bushel lower at $2.93.
Gold prices rose partly on support from news that a huge gold deposit in Indonesia would not pan out. June gold at the Commodity Exchange closed at $344.30 an ounce, up $2.70.

Canadian consultants Strathcona Mineral Services Ltd said in a report issued on Sunday that gold assay results for the Busang deposit in Indonesia had been falsified on a scale "without precedent in the history of mining."

That deposit just two months ago had been called "the find of the century," so traders bought gold encouraged by the idea that the 71 million ounces of gold mine supply that had been estimated at Busang would not now come to market.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil prices ended slightly higher as ethnic clashes in Nigeria continued to disrupt oil production there. Crude oil for May delivery rose 3 cents a barrel to close at $19.63.
"It's a real thin market, but troubles in Nigeria created some short-covering early," said Al Lindesth, manager of oil and gas hedge programs at GSC Energy in Atlanta.

Nigeria's semi-official newspaper the Daily Times on Saturday quoted the country's oil minister Dan Etete as saying a 125,000 barrel per day oil refinery in the city of Warri had been shut following recent ethnic clashes.
Etete said a fuel shortage could hit western Nigeria if the facility was not reopened soon.
But some dealers played down the significance of Monday's trading since a British holiday shut trading in London and contributed to light volumes in New York.
June unleaded gasoline closed 0.02 cent a gallon higher at 60.54 cents and June heating oil rose 0.03 cent a gallon to close at 53.05 cents.
